One bank balance, several promises: stop counting the same savings more than once

Compare requested earmarks with money actually available, then use a payment calendar to find whether future deposits arrive before the cash is needed.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Check several earmarks against one real cash balance

Interactive planning lab

Opening claims beyond the actual bank balance$5,000
Extra starting cash needed to preserve the floor at every date$1,000
Bank cash remaining after twelve months$13,000

Original hypothetical twelve-month cash ledger. There is one starting bank balance, not a separate copy for each earmark. Opening allocations use an illustrative order: protect the selected floor, then assign the required bill, then the planned purchase, each only from remaining cash. This order is not a legal priority or an optimized plan. All bills are nevertheless paid in full on their selected month; negative balances are unfunded needs, not automatic borrowing. New monthly money arrives before that month’s bills, and same-month bills are added. The protected floor is held as cash throughout, not paid away as another bill. Cash earns zero. Required bill and purchase amounts are independently entered, with no tax calculation, credit, fees, refund, return or other household expenses. The additional starting cash covers the lowest cash point relative to the floor, not just the final balance.

The central idea

Naming a bank balance an emergency fund, a tax reserve and a purchase fund does not create three balances. Reconcile all claims to the same cash and then check the payment dates.

01

Separate a purpose label from an additional asset

Suppose a household sees CAD 30,000 in a bank account and mentally describes it as enough for a CAD 12,000 emergency reserve. Later, the same statement seems sufficient for a CAD 9,000 bill. A planned CAD 14,000 purchase also looks smaller than the displayed balance. Each statement can appear reasonable in isolation while the three claims together exceed the cash.

The combined requirement is CAD 35,000. Only CAD 30,000 exists at the start, so the full claims are overcommitted by CAD 5,000. Repeating the balance beside each goal does not make the difference available.

The FCAC’s budgeting guidance treats saving goals as part of the same plan as income and expenses. This article applies that idea to money already accumulated. It does not prescribe a reserve size or decide which personal goal should receive priority.

02

Allocate existing money once, in an explicit order

The opening-allocation bars use a stated illustrative order: assign cash to the protected floor, then the required bill, then the planned purchase. This is an accounting convention for the example, not a legal priority rule or an optimized recommendation.

The first CAD 12,000 is assigned to the floor, leaving CAD 18,000. The required bill receives CAD 9,000, leaving CAD 9,000. The purchase requests CAD 14,000 but can be assigned only the remaining CAD 9,000. Its opening funding gap is therefore CAD 5,000.

The three assigned amounts add to CAD 30,000, exactly the actual balance. Another order could move the unfunded amount to a different purpose; it would not eliminate the total shortage. A dedicated bank subaccount can make an assignment easier to track, but a transfer between a household’s own accounts does not create new resources. Reconcile the combined balances and assignments once.

03

Understand what the opening waterfall subtracts

The opening waterfall begins with the real bank balance and subtracts all requested claims. Its negative CAD 5,000 endpoint describes unassigned capacity after those full requests. It is not the bank’s actual closing balance, because no bill has been paid merely by writing down the earmarks.

This distinction matters when reviewing a household balance sheet. Earmarked cash remains an asset. A planned expense is a future use of that asset. Subtracting the cash from net worth when it is labelled, and then subtracting the later bill again, would count the same use twice.

The allocation test deliberately ignores future income. It answers whether all the purposes can be funded immediately from current cash. The next chart adds a separate calendar to answer whether new money can close the gap before each bill. Passing that second test does not mean the opening claims were fully funded at the start.

04

Future saving helps only before the relevant payment

The default calendar adds CAD 500 of new money before each month’s bills. It pays the required CAD 9,000 bill in month four and the CAD 14,000 purchase in month eight. The CAD 12,000 protected floor is a reference amount retained as cash throughout, not a third bill paid away.

After the required bill, the account holds CAD 23,000. By month eight, new saving and the purchase payment leave CAD 11,000. That is still a positive bank balance, but it is CAD 1,000 below the selected protected floor. At year-end, the account has recovered to CAD 13,000.

A year-end review would therefore miss the earlier use of the protected money. The calendar needs CAD 1,000 of extra starting cash to stay at or above the floor at every modeled date. That is different from the CAD 5,000 opening allocation shortage: four thousand dollars of new saving has arrived by the purchase date, reducing the funding problem before the bill is paid.

05

Test the floor, purchase size and new-money assumption

The matrix changes the planned-purchase amount and monthly new money. Starting cash, the selected floor, the required bill and both payment months stay fixed. Each cell measures additional starting cash needed to preserve the floor at every date, including time zero.

If both bills fall in the same month, the ledger adds them before testing the remaining cash. If a bill actually arrives before that month’s income, a more detailed daily calendar may require additional accessible cash. The modeled order of receipts before bills should therefore be checked against real dates.

The tool pays entered bills in full even if the balance becomes negative. That negative amount identifies an unfunded need; it is not an assumed overdraft approval, credit line or permission to miss another payment. No borrowing interest is hidden in the chart. Changing or postponing a purchase would require an explicit new scenario.

06

Keep one source of truth for cash assigned to goals

Start with a dated statement balance for money that is actually accessible. List every purpose already claiming part of it. Confirm bill amounts and dates independently; the field labelled required bill can represent a tax payment, but this tool neither determines tax owed nor establishes its due date.

Record an amount as assigned, still unfunded or paid. When a bill is paid, reduce both bank cash and its outstanding claim so that a completed expense does not remain in the future budget. When new saving arrives, assign it once. Interest, refunds or transfers should be added only when the plan has supported amounts and receipt dates.

Use the four views together: requested versus assigned money, total opening capacity, the real cash calendar and alternative funding assumptions. A reserve is useful only to the extent that the cash remains available when needed. A good set of labels helps reveal that availability; the labels themselves cannot supply it.
